claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and exhibits brittle behavior.
Concentrated dislocation pile-ups at sharp internal boundaries cause the untreated alloy's limited ductility and brittleness.
The proposed intervention is solution treatment at 1100 °C for 1 hour, quenching, and aging at 500–550 °C for 4–6 hours under an inert atmosphere.
The proposed heat treatment will produce nanoscale coherent precipitates along the lamellar phase boundaries.
Aging promotes nucleation of fine precipitates at internal boundaries.
The boundary precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The precipitates disrupt concentrated dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
Disrupting dislocation pile-ups distributes plastic deformation more uniformly.
More uniform plastic deformation reduces local stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle failure.
The aged alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The aged alloy will maintain or increase its yield and ultimate tensile strengths relative to the untreated alloy.
Precipitation strengthening is responsible for maintaining or increasing yield and ultimate tensile strengths.
The predicted effects apply to tensile loading at room temperature and a strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility changes depends on precipitate density, size, and distribution.
The treatment's performance under extreme environments or high strain rates is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The prediction permits strength to be maintained, whereas the falsification rule treats 'no increase' in strength as part of a failure condition. In addition, its conjunction means that failure of only the ductility prediction or only the strength prediction may not falsify the hypothesis.
